verdict: Caution — lend selectively to domestic-focused mid-size BPO/KPO and medical-coding firms with diversified client bases and clean labour records; avoid single-client, US-concentrated vendors and any account with unresolved retrenchment disputes.
title: Thiruvananthapuram IT-enabled services & BPO: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**These firms sell trained people and process discipline, not products.** A BPO or medical-coding unit converts seats, software licences and supervisory layers into monthly invoices to overseas clients, mostly US healthcare and financial-services payers. So when a proposal lands, check the client-concentration schedule first; if one client is above a third of revenue, ask for the contract tenure and exit clause.

## What has changed now
**The local shock is labour, not demand.** A US-based medical-coding firm retrenched staff in Kerala and CITU has moved to raise it as an industrial dispute before the Labour Commissioner and Labour Courts [1]; reports put the cut at 850 employees across Kochi and Kozhikode [2]. Note this is a state-level labour story, not a Thiruvananthapuram-specific one — the sources say little about this city's own establishment base, so lean on first principles here. **On the demand side, peers are holding up unevenly:** eClerx grew revenue 17.1% YoY to INR 1,212.6 crore in Q2 FY2026-27 [5], while Hinduja Global Solutions grew just 1.1% YoY to Rs 1,075.4 crore with EBITDA margin down to 11.2% from 19.0% [6]. TCS held operating margin at 24% and Infosys at 21% [7] — but those are large-cap IT services, not BPO comparables. **Read the spread as: analytics-led work is growing, plain-vanilla voice/BPO is flat and margin-squeezed.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue domestic-demand and India-delivery BPO/KPO units, and medical-coding firms with multi-payer, multi-client books.** The YOO Hub Trivandrum project at Technopark Phase III is projected to add 5,000 jobs [3] — that is a pipeline signal for landlord-linked and staffing-linked lending, not proof of tenant credit. **Avoid single-client captives and any vendor whose revenue is one US payer.** The 850-job cut [2] shows how fast a concentrated book becomes a labour liability.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the receivable, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly MIS: client-wise revenue, attrition, seat utilisation, debtor days and salary-run coverage. Ask for monthly ESI/PF remittance proof — a missed remittance is the earliest sign of a cash crunch in this industry. **Covenant on client concentration and on labour compliance:** if a borrower's top client exceeds the agreed share, reprice or reduce limit. Where the figure is missing, collect from customer.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch attrition and bench strength monthly.** Rising bench with flat billing means margin erosion before it shows in the P&L. **Watch for dispute filings and union activity** — the CITU route to the Labour Commissioner [1] is a public record you can check quarterly. **Watch debtor days and any request to fund salaries** — that is the classic pre-default pattern in this sector.
watch: missed or part remittance -> freeze fresh disbursement and call for cash-flow statement
top client above agreed share -> reprice limit or seek additional collateral
bench rising with flat billing -> ask for revised margin projection and tighten drawing power
dispute filed before Labour Commissioner -> reassess account and seek client-contract tenure proof
debtor days stretching or salary funding request -> treat as stress signal, reduce exposure
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
